benedikt-gruendet-montecassino#text: Benedict of Nursia had lived as a hermit near Subiaco before founding a monastery around 529 on the mountain of Cassino between Rome and Naples. For his community he wrote a Rule that divided the monks' day between prayer, reading and manual work, demanded moderation and obedience, and made the abbot the father of the community. Over the following centuries the Rule of Benedict prevailed in almost all monasteries of Western Europe. Monasteries such as Monte Cassino, Fulda, St. Gall and Cluny became centers of agriculture, nursing and the art of writing, where ancient manuscripts were preserved.
justinian-und-hagia-sophia#summary: In Constantinople the largest church in the world is built in just five years, a symbol of the power of the Eastern Roman emperor Justinian.
justinian-und-hagia-sophia#text: After the Nika riot destroyed the old church in 532, Justinian had the mathematicians Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus build a structure with a seemingly floating dome more than 30 meters across. At the consecration on 27 December 537 he is said to have exclaimed that he had surpassed Solomon. In those same years Justinian had Roman law compiled in the Corpus Iuris Civilis, which shapes the legal order of Europe to this day, and with his generals Belisarius and Narses he reconquered North Africa and Italy. The Hagia Sophia was the largest church in Christendom for almost a thousand years, became a mosque in 1453 and is today a landmark of Istanbul.
wari-reich#summary: From Ayacucho the Wari build the first great empire of the Andes.
wari-reich#text: The capital of the Wari lay near Ayacucho in the highlands of Peru. From there they dominated large parts of today's Peru between about 600 and 1000. They built planned administrative centers such as Pikillacta near Cusco, constructed roads and terraces and already used knotted cords for bookkeeping. Many researchers therefore see the Wari as forerunners of the Inca administration. Their art shares motifs such as the Staff God with Tiwanaku, with which they had both peaceful and hostile contact.
erste-offenbarung-mohammeds#summary: In a cave on Mount Hira near Mecca, Muhammad receives the first revelation according to Islamic tradition.
erste-offenbarung-mohammeds#text: Muhammad, a merchant of about forty from the Quraysh tribe, regularly withdrew to a cave on Mount Hira to reflect. There, according to Muslim belief, the angel Gabriel appeared to him with the charge to proclaim the words of God. The revelations he received until his death were later collected in the Quran. His preaching of the one God and of responsibility toward the poor and the weak won him his first followers but brought him into conflict with the leading families of Mecca, who profited from the worship of the old gods at the Kaaba.
pakal-herrscht-in-palenque#summary: Under King Pakal, Palenque reaches its greatest flowering; his tomb is among the most important finds of Maya research.
pakal-herrscht-in-palenque#text: Pakal ascended the throne of Palenque in 615 at the age of twelve, after his mother Sak K'uk' had ruled before him. During his reign of almost 70 years, the city recovered from defeats by Calakmul and became a leading kingdom in the west of the Maya region. He had the palace enlarged and the Temple of the Inscriptions built, whose texts tell the history of his dynasty. In 1952 Alberto Ruz Lhuillier discovered the burial chamber inside the pyramid with its richly carved sarcophagus and a death mask of jade.
tang-dynastie#title: The Beginning of the Tang Dynasty
tang-dynastie#summary: The Tang dynasty makes China the most powerful and most cosmopolitan empire of its time.
tang-dynastie#text: Li Yuan founded the Tang dynasty in 618, under which China was a cultural and political great power for almost three centuries. The capital Chang'an, with about a million inhabitants, hosted merchants, monks and envoys from Persia, India, Korea and Japan. The poets Li Bai and Du Fu, woodblock printing and the civil service examinations define the image of this period; in Wu Zetian, the only woman in Chinese history reigned as empress in her own right. After the rebellion of An Lushan from 755, the court gradually lost control of the provinces.
hidschra-nach-medina#summary: Muhammad and his followers migrate from Mecca to Medina; the Islamic calendar begins with this year.
hidschra-nach-medina#text: Because of growing hostility in Mecca, Muhammad and his companions accepted an invitation in 622 from the oasis of Yathrib, which from then on was called Medina, the city of the Prophet. There Muhammad became the religious and political head of a community that he bound to the resident tribes in a community charter. After several battles with the Meccans he returned to Mecca in 630 almost without a fight and dedicated the Kaaba to the one God. The caliph Umar later fixed the Hijra as the beginning of the Islamic calendar.
schlacht-von-badr#summary: The small Muslim community from Medina defeats a considerably larger Meccan army at the oasis of Badr.
schlacht-von-badr#text: Two years after the Hijra, in March 624, the first great battle between Muhammad's followers and the leading families of Mecca took place at the oasis of Badr southwest of Medina. About 300 Muslims faced some 1,000 Meccans who had marched out to protect a trade caravan, and nevertheless won a clear victory in which several of their fiercest opponents fell. For the Muslims, Badr was a sign of divine support and considerably strengthened Muhammad's standing in Medina and among the tribes of Arabia. There followed the defeat at Uhud in 625 and the successful defense of Medina at the Battle of the Trench in 627, before Muhammad won Mecca in 630.
arabische-eroberung-jerusalems#summary: The Byzantine city of Jerusalem surrenders to the caliph Umar, who guarantees protection to Christians and Jews.
arabische-eroberung-jerusalems#text: After the victory over the Byzantines at the Yarmuk River in 636, Arab troops besieged Jerusalem, which the patriarch Sophronius handed over personally to the caliph Umar in 638. Umar guaranteed the Christians possession of their churches and once again allowed Jews, after centuries, to settle in the city. On the Temple Mount the Dome of the Rock was later built, completed in 691 and among the oldest Islamic structures. Jerusalem thus became a holy city of all three Abrahamic religions and remained under Muslim rule for more than 450 years.
baqt-vertrag-makuria#title: The Baqt treaty between Makuria and Egypt
baqt-vertrag-makuria#summary: The Christian Nubian kingdom of Makuria repels the Arab armies and concludes a treaty with Egypt that remains in force for about 600 years.
baqt-vertrag-makuria#text: After the conquest of Egypt, Arab troops advanced up the Nile but in 652 failed in the siege of Dongola, the capital of Makuria, against the feared Nubian archers. Both sides then concluded the Baqt, a treaty of peace and exchange: Nubia delivered a fixed number of slaves each year, Egypt grain, cloth and other goods. The agreement secured Makuria centuries of independence as a Christian kingdom. Churches such as the cathedral of Faras with its colorful wall paintings bear witness to the flowering of Nubian culture. Only in the 14th century did the kingdom decline.
umayyaden-kalifat-in-damaskus#summary: Muawiya founds the first caliphal dynasty and makes Damascus the capital of an empire reaching from Spain to the Indus.
umayyaden-kalifat-in-damaskus#text: After the murder of the fourth caliph Ali, the governor of Syria, Muawiya, prevailed and turned the caliphate into a hereditary office of his family. The dispute over the rightful succession to the Prophet led to the split into Sunnis and Shiites that persists to this day. Under the Umayyads, Arab armies conquered North Africa, in 711 the Visigothic kingdom in Spain, and territories as far as Central Asia and the Indus. Arabic became the language of administration, distinct gold coins were minted, and the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus was created as a masterpiece of Islamic architecture.
schlacht-von-kerbela#summary: Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, is killed with his companions by troops of the Umayyad caliph Yazid; the division between Sunnis and Shiites deepens.
schlacht-von-kerbela#text: After the death of the caliph Muawiya in 680, his son Yazid succeeded him, which many Muslims saw as a break with the election of the caliph. Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of Muhammad and son of the fourth caliph Ali, set out with his family and a few dozen companions for Kufa in Iraq, where supporters had invited him to lead them. On 10 October 680 the small group was surrounded at Karbala by a vastly superior army, cut off from the water source and killed after a final fight. For the Shiites, the followers of Ali and his descendants, Husayn became a martyr; they commemorate his death every year on the day of Ashura, and Karbala is one of their most important places of pilgrimage.
frau-sechs-himmel-in-naranjo#title: Lady Six Sky renews the dynasty of Naranjo
frau-sechs-himmel-in-naranjo#summary: A princess from Dos Pilas comes to Naranjo and becomes the most powerful person in the kingdom.
frau-sechs-himmel-in-naranjo#text: In 682 Lady Six Sky, a daughter of the king of Dos Pilas, arrived at Naranjo, whose royal house had been weakened by defeats. Inscriptions celebrated her arrival as a new beginning for the dynasty. In 693 her five-year-old son was crowned king, but for years real power lay with her. Stelae show her in royal dress standing over captured enemies and report military campaigns in her time. She is one of the best-known female rulers of the Maya.
wu-zetian-wird-kaiserin#title: Wu Zetian Becomes Empress of China
wu-zetian-wird-kaiserin#summary: The emperor's former concubine proclaims a dynasty of her own and rules as the only woman in Chinese history to reign in her own right.
wu-zetian-wird-kaiserin#text: Wu Zetian was a concubine of two emperors and, after her husband Gaozong fell ill, directed the government from 660; after his death she stripped her sons of power. In 690 she had herself proclaimed emperor, founded the Zhou dynasty and based her rule on Buddhism, which celebrated her as the return of a bodhisattva. She promoted the civil service examinations, brought capable men from simple families into government, and expanded the empire toward Korea and Central Asia. In 705 a palace coup forced her, then over eighty, to abdicate, and the Tang dynasty was restored.
tikal-besiegt-calakmul#summary: In the struggle between the two Maya great powers, Tikal wins a decisive victory over the Snake kingdom.
tikal-besiegt-calakmul#text: For more than a century Tikal and Calakmul, the Snake kingdom, struggled for supremacy in the Maya lowlands. In 562 Calakmul and its allies had defeated Tikal, after which no monuments were erected there for a long time. In 695 King Jasaw Chan K'awiil beat the army of the Calakmul king Yich'aak K'ahk' and celebrated the victory with festivals and carved wooden lintels. Calakmul never fully recovered, while Tikal enjoyed a new flowering. The wars show how strongly alliances and vassal relationships shaped Maya politics.
belagerung-konstantinopels-717#summary: A large Umayyad army and fleet besiege the Byzantine capital for a year but founder on its walls, on Greek fire and on the winter.
belagerung-konstantinopels-717#text: After conquering Syria, Egypt and North Africa, the Umayyads wanted to subdue Christian Byzantium as well, whose capital they had already besieged in vain from 674 to 678. In the summer of 717 the commander Maslama encircled Constantinople with a land army and hundreds of ships, and the new emperor Leo III defended it vigorously. Byzantine ships destroyed the Arab fleet with Greek fire, a burning liquid; an unusually harsh winter and epidemics decimated the besiegers, and the Bulgars attacked the Arab camp. In August 718 Maslama broke off the siege; Byzantium endured for another seven centuries and remained the barrier between the caliphate and southeastern Europe.
schlacht-bei-tours-und-poitiers#title: The Battle of Tours and Poitiers
schlacht-bei-tours-und-poitiers#summary: The Frankish mayor of the palace Charles Martel defeats an Arab-Berber army and halts the advance northward.
schlacht-bei-tours-und-poitiers#text: From Spain, Muslim armies repeatedly pushed across the Pyrenees into southern France. In October 732, Charles Martel confronted the governor Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi with his Frankish infantry between Tours and Poitiers; the Arab leader fell and his army withdrew. The significance of the battle was often exaggerated later, but it strengthened the position of the Carolingians, who gained the Frankish crown a few decades afterwards. Muslim rule remained confined to the Iberian Peninsula, where it lasted almost 800 more years.
abbasiden-revolution#summary: A revolt from Khurasan overthrows the Umayyads; the Abbasids take over the caliphate and shift the empire's center eastward.
abbasiden-revolution#text: Umayyad rule was hated by many non-Arab Muslims, above all Persians, because despite their conversion to Islam they paid higher taxes and remained excluded from office; the Shiites and many pious Arabs rejected the dynasty as well. The Abbasids, descendants of an uncle of the Prophet, gathered these discontented groups, and in 747 troops rose under the commander Abu Muslim in Khurasan beneath black banners. In January 750 they defeated the Umayyad army at the Great Zab in Iraq, the last Umayyad caliph Marwan II was killed while fleeing in Egypt, and almost the entire family fell victim to a massacre. Only Abd al-Rahman escaped to Spain, where he founded the Emirate of Córdoba in 756. The Abbasids opened administration and court to Persians and other peoples and, with Baghdad, made Iraq the center of the Islamic world.
gruendung-bagdads#summary: The Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founds a new capital on the Tigris that becomes the largest city in the world.
gruendung-bagdads#text: After the Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads in 750, the caliph al-Mansur had a circular royal city built on the Tigris, which he called Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace. Its favorable position on the trade routes between Persia, India, Arabia and the Mediterranean made Baghdad grow quickly; by around 900 more than half a million people probably lived there. Markets, libraries, hospitals and mosques made the city the center of the Islamic world. The tales of the Thousand and One Nights reflect the splendor of Abbasid Baghdad.
ueberfall-auf-lindisfarne#title: The Raid on Lindisfarne: the Beginning of the Viking Age
ueberfall-auf-lindisfarne#summary: Scandinavian seafarers plunder the monastery of Lindisfarne off the English coast and cause horror across Europe.
ueberfall-auf-lindisfarne#text: On 8 June 793, Vikings landed on the island of Lindisfarne, killed monks, stole church treasures and carried off captives. The attack is regarded as the beginning of the Viking Age, in which Northmen with their fast longships raided coasts and rivers from England to the Mediterranean. They were at the same time traders, explorers and settlers: they founded Dublin and Normandy, controlled trade routes to Russia and Byzantium, and around 1000 reached Iceland, Greenland and North America.
heian-zeit-in-japan#summary: With the move of the capital to Heian-kyo, today's Kyoto, the classical court culture of Japan begins.
heian-zeit-in-japan#text: Emperor Kanmu moved the court to Heian-kyo in 794 to escape the influence of the powerful Buddhist monasteries of Nara. The noble Fujiwara family effectively governed in place of the emperors for centuries. At court the Japanese syllabaries were created, along with works such as The Tale of Genji by the lady-in-waiting Murasaki Shikibu, regarded as the first novel in world literature. When the warrior families of the Minamoto and the Taira fought for power, the era ended in 1185 with the establishment of the first shogunate.
kollaps-der-klassischen-maya#title: The collapse of the Classic Maya cities
kollaps-der-klassischen-maya#summary: In the 9th century the great royal cities in the southern Maya lowlands are abandoned.
kollaps-der-klassischen-maya#text: From about 800 the inscriptions ceased in one city after another, palaces were abandoned and the population of the southern lowlands declined sharply. The last known Long Count date comes from Toniná in 909. Recurring droughts, overuse of soils and forests, constant wars and the loss of faith in the divine kings are considered causes. The Maya themselves did not vanish: in northern Yucatán cities such as Chichén Itzá continued to flourish, and millions of people still speak Maya languages today.
kaiserkroenung-karls-des-grossen#summary: Pope Leo III crowns the Frankish king emperor in Rome on Christmas Day and renews the Western empire.
kaiserkroenung-karls-des-grossen#text: Charlemagne had built the Frankish kingdom through wars against Lombards, Saxons and Avars into the largest realm in Western Europe since Rome. When he protected Pope Leo III against his Roman opponents, the pope placed the imperial crown on his head in St. Peter's on 25 December 800. With that the West again claimed an empire of its own alongside Byzantium. Charlemagne reorganized administration, coinage and church, had schools founded and a new, easily legible script developed; this is known as the Carolingian Renaissance.
al-chwarizmi-begruendet-die-algebra#summ: The mathematician al-Khwarizmi writes a textbook in Baghdad on solving equations, from whose title the word algebra comes.
al-chwarizmi-begruendet-die-algebra#text: Around 820, Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote at the court of the caliph al-Mamun The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing, in Arabic al-jabr wa'l-muqabala. In it he showed step by step how equations of the first and second degree can be solved, and explained their application to inheritance division, trade and land surveying; from al-jabr came the word algebra. In a second work he explained calculation with the Indian numerals and zero, which spread through Europe in Latin translation under his name as algorismus; from this came the term algorithm. Al-Khwarizmi also calculated astronomical tables and wrote a work of geography with the coordinates of more than 2,000 places.
haus-der-weisheit#title: The House of Wisdom in Baghdad
haus-der-weisheit#summary: Under the caliph al-Mamun, Baghdad becomes a center of translation and scholarship.
haus-der-weisheit#text: Harun al-Rashid had already built up a library in Baghdad; his son al-Mamun expanded it into an academy in which scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian writings into Arabic. The mathematician al-Khwarizmi wrote his textbook on calculating with equations here, from whose title the word algebra and from whose name the term algorithm arose. Astronomers measured the circumference of the Earth, and physicians such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated Galen and Hippocrates. The numerals with zero taken over from India spread from here throughout the Islamic world and later to Europe.
vertrag-von-verdun#summary: The grandsons of Charlemagne divide the Frankish empire into three parts; from West and East Francia, France and Germany emerge.
vertrag-von-verdun#text: After the death of Louis the Pious in 840, his sons fought over the inheritance until they agreed on a partition at Verdun in 843: Charles the Bald received the west, Louis the German the east, and Lothair I, who held the imperial title, an elongated middle kingdom stretching from the North Sea to Italy. The year before, Charles and Louis had sworn their alliance in the Oaths of Strasbourg in Old French and Old High German, the oldest surviving texts in either language. The middle kingdom soon broke apart and remained a bone of contention between its neighbors into the 20th century, while the East and West Frankish kingdoms developed into Germany and France.
aufstieg-von-chichen-itza#summary: In northern Yucatán, Chichén Itzá becomes the leading city of the Maya world.
aufstieg-von-chichen-itza#text: While the cities of the south declined, Chichén Itzá rose to dominance in the north of the Yucatán peninsula. Its landmark is the pyramid of Kukulkan, the feathered serpent, on whose staircase a play of shadows resembling a serpent's body appears at the equinoxes. The city has the largest ball court in Mesoamerica and a sacred cenote, a natural well into which offerings of gold, jade and human beings were thrown. Architectural forms and images resemble those of Tula and show close contacts with central Mexico. Later Mayapán took over the leadership in Yucatán.
grosshaeuser-im-chaco-canyon#title: The great houses of Chaco Canyon
grosshaeuser-im-chaco-canyon#summary: The Ancestral Puebloans build multistory structures and a wide network of roads in southwestern North America.
grosshaeuser-im-chaco-canyon#text: In Chaco Canyon in present-day New Mexico, large multistory stone buildings were erected between about 850 and 1150. The largest, Pueblo Bonito, had hundreds of rooms and round ceremonial chambers, the kivas. Straight roads led to outlying settlements, and finds of turquoise, macaws and cacao bear witness to trade reaching as far as Mesoamerica. After a long drought Chaco lost its importance; later the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde arose, which were likewise abandoned around 1300. The descendants of the builders live today among the Hopi, Zuni and other Pueblo peoples.
diamant-sutra-holztafeldruck#title: The Diamond Sutra: the oldest dated printed book
diamant-sutra-holztafeldruck#summary: A Buddhist text is printed from woodblocks in China; it is still regarded as the oldest dated printed work in the world.
diamant-sutra-holztafeldruck#text: The Diamond Sutra is a scroll five meters long, made of seven sheets pasted together, whose closing note records that a certain Wang Jie had it made on 11 May 868 in memory of his parents. Text and a frontispiece were cut in mirror image into wooden blocks, inked, and pressed onto paper; the technique had been in use in China since the 7th century for amulets and calendars. The scroll lay for more than a thousand years in a walled-up cave near Dunhuang, until the explorer Aurel Stein acquired it in 1907; today it is kept in the British Library. In the 11th century Bi Sheng in China also invented movable type made of clay.
chan-chan-hauptstadt-der-chimu#title: Chan Chan, the capital of the Chimú
chan-chan-hauptstadt-der-chimu#summary: On the north coast of Peru the largest adobe city in the Americas arises.
chan-chan-hauptstadt-der-chimu#text: The kingdom of Chimor, whose inhabitants are called Chimú, dominated a long stretch of Peru's coast from the 10th to the 15th century. Its capital Chan Chan near Trujillo was built of adobe bricks and covered many square kilometers. High walls enclosed large palace compounds of the kings with courtyards, storerooms and burial platforms, decorated with reliefs of fish, birds and waves. The Chimú were famous metalworkers and built extensive irrigation systems. Around 1470 the Inca conquered the kingdom and brought its goldsmiths to Cusco.
tula-hauptstadt-der-tolteken#title: Tula, the city of the Toltecs
tula-hauptstadt-der-tolteken#summary: North of the Valley of Mexico, Tula becomes the center of the Toltecs, whom the Aztecs later regarded as exemplary ancestors.
tula-hauptstadt-der-tolteken#text: After the decline of Teotihuacan, Tula in today's state of Hidalgo became the most important city of central Mexico. On a temple pyramid the stone warrior figures more than four meters tall, the so-called Atlanteans, still stand today. Reliefs with jaguars, eagles and skull racks show the importance of war and sacrifice. Around 1150 the city was destroyed or abandoned. The Aztecs later glorified the Toltecs as the inventors of all the arts and derived the dignity of their own rulers from them.
kalifat-von-cordoba#summary: Abd al-Rahman III proclaims himself caliph in Spain and makes Córdoba the most splendid city in Europe.
kalifat-von-cordoba#text: After the fall of the Umayyads in Damascus, a fugitive of the dynasty had founded an emirate of his own in Spain. In 929 Abd al-Rahman III assumed the title of caliph, placing himself on a par with the Abbasids in Baghdad and the Fatimids in North Africa. Córdoba had paved and lighted streets, baths, hundreds of mosques, and a library said to hold 400,000 volumes; in the palace city of Madinat al-Zahra the caliph received envoys from Byzantium and the Frankish empire. Muslims, Jews, and Christians long lived together in al-Andalus in relative peace. In 1031 the caliphate broke apart into numerous small kingdoms.
schlacht-auf-dem-lechfeld#title: Otto I triumphs at the Lechfeld
schlacht-auf-dem-lechfeld#summary: The East Frankish king defeats the Hungarians near Augsburg and is crowned emperor seven years later.
schlacht-auf-dem-lechfeld#text: Since the end of the 9th century, mounted Hungarian warriors had plundered central Europe almost every year. When they besieged Augsburg in 955, which Bishop Ulrich was defending, Otto I led an army drawn from all the tribes of the realm against them on 10 August and won a complete victory at the Lechfeld. The Hungarians then settled permanently in the Pannonian plain and adopted Christianity around 1000. Otto's standing was now so great that Pope John XII crowned him emperor in Rome in 962; this was the beginning of the Holy Roman Empire, which lasted until 1806.
fatimiden-gruenden-kairo#title: The Fatimids found Cairo and al-Azhar
fatimiden-gruenden-kairo#summary: The Shiite Fatimids conquer Egypt, found the royal city of al-Qahira, and build the al-Azhar mosque as a place of learning.
fatimiden-gruenden-kairo#text: The Fatimids, a Shiite dynasty that traced its descent from Fatima, the daughter of the Prophet, had established a caliphate of their own in North Africa in 909. In 969 their general Jawhar conquered Egypt and had a new palace city laid out north of the old capital Fustat, which was given the name al-Qahira, the victorious; from this came Cairo. From 970 the al-Azhar mosque was built there, where jurists and theologians soon taught; it is regarded as one of the oldest universities still in existence. Under the Fatimids, Cairo became the richest center of the Islamic world, with libraries, markets, and trade across the Red Sea to India; after the dynasty ended in 1171, Saladin made al-Azhar a Sunni institution of learning, which it remains to this day.
chola-reich-in-suedindien#title: Rise of the Chola empire in South India
chola-reich-in-suedindien#summary: Under Rajaraja I and Rajendra I, the Cholas become the leading land and sea power of the Indian Ocean.
chola-reich-in-suedindien#text: Rajaraja I ascended the Chola throne in the Tamil south of India in 985, subdued the neighboring kingdoms and Sri Lanka, and had the enormous Brihadishvara temple to Shiva built at Thanjavur. His son Rajendra I sent an army as far as the Ganges and, in 1025, a fleet against the kingdom of Srivijaya on Sumatra in order to control the sea routes to China. The Cholas governed their empire through village assemblies whose decisions are recorded in temple inscriptions, and their bronze sculptors created the dancing Shiva Nataraja, a masterpiece of world art. The empire broke apart in the 13th century.
christianisierung-der-kiewer-rus#summary: Grand Prince Vladimir is baptized and makes Orthodox Christianity the religion of his realm on the Dnieper.
christianisierung-der-kiewer-rus#text: Kievan Rus had emerged in the 9th century from Scandinavian merchant-warriors, the Varangians, and Slavic tribes, and it controlled the trade route from the Baltic to Byzantium. Vladimir I was baptized in 988, married Anna, the sister of the Byzantine emperor Basil II, and had the population of Kiev baptized in the Dnieper. With the faith came the Cyrillic script, canon law, icon painting, and master builders from Byzantium; under Yaroslav the Wise the Cathedral of Saint Sophia in Kiev and the first law code were created. Rus thus became the cradle of Russian, Ukrainian, and Belarusian culture, until the Mongols destroyed Kiev in 1240.
genji-monogatari#title: Murasaki Shikibu completes The Tale of Genji
genji-monogatari#summary: At the Japanese imperial court, a lady-in-waiting writes the story of Prince Genji, regarded as the first novel in world literature.
genji-monogatari#text: Murasaki Shikibu served Empress Shoshi at the court of Heian-kyo, where she wrote the story of Prince Genji, his love affairs, and his descendants in 54 chapters, using the Japanese syllabary. Her diary mentions the work for the first time in 1008, when parts of it were already being read aloud at court. With a fine feeling for emotion, the seasons, and transience, the novel depicts the courtly world of the Heian period, and in Japan it was copied, illustrated, and annotated for centuries. At the same time her rival Sei Shonagon wrote The Pillow Book, a collection of observations and lists.
song-dynastie-erfindungen#title: The Song dynasty: gunpowder, compass, and paper money
